label: Sexual Purity and Desire
framing: Scripture takes desire seriously precisely because it takes the body seriously, treating sex not as dirty but as so weighty it belongs inside covenant. Purity in the Bible is not the absence of desire but desire rightly ordered, aimed at the place it was made for.
cultural: The Greco-Roman world held a casual view of male appetite, where a man's use of slaves and others outside marriage was simply assumed. Into that, the early Christians made a startling demand, the same standard for men as for women, fidelity inside marriage and faithfulness outside it, which struck the ancient world as strange and which our own age, having returned to the older license under a newer name, finds strange again.
historical: Paul wrote of fleeing sexual immorality to a Corinth famous for it, and the church's sexual ethic was, in the ancient world, a liberation rather than a repression, especially for the women and the powerless it protected. Augustine, who knew the pull of disordered desire from the inside before his conversion in 386, wrote with rare honesty about the divided will, and the tradition has held both the goodness of the body and the discipline of its longings ever since.
application: Treat your desires as real and good and in need of direction rather than denial or surrender. Guard the inputs, since what you feed the imagination shapes what the body wants. Walk in the light with someone who can ask you hard questions, since secrecy is where every appetite goes feral. And remember that the call to self-control is not God begrudging you joy but guarding a thing strong enough to wound you.

verses.text: And the man and his wife were both naked, and they were not ashamed.
verses.where: The second creation story ends with the first marriage: a man and a woman joined as one flesh, naked and not ashamed. The body and its desire are part of the world God called good. The very next scene is the one in which shame enters and they hide.

verses.text: O daughters of Jerusalem, I adjure you by the gazelles and does of the field: Do not arouse or awaken love until the time is right.
verses.where: The Bible's love poem celebrates desire between a man and a woman without embarrassment. In the middle of that celebration the woman charges her friends not to stir up love before its time. The Song honors desire and asks for patience with it in the same breath.

verses.text: May your fountain be blessed, and may you rejoice in the wife of your youth: A loving doe, a graceful fawn— may her breasts satisfy you always; may you be captivated by her love forever.
verses.where: A father warns his son about a woman whose words are sweet at first and bitter in the end. His answer is not to despise desire but to give it a home: find delight in the wife of your youth. The chapter adds that every path a man takes is before the eyes of the LORD.

verses.text: Jesus answered, “Have you not read that from the beginning the Creator ‘made them male and female,’ and said, ‘For this reason a man will leave his father and mother and be united to his wife, and the two will become one flesh’? So they are no longer two, but one flesh. Therefore what God has joined together, let man not separate.”
verses.where: Pharisees test Jesus on whether a man may divorce his wife for any reason. He answers by going behind Moses to creation, joining Genesis 1 and Genesis 2: God made them male and female, and the two become one flesh. The question was about a husband's rights; Jesus turns it to God's design.

verses.text: For it is God’s will that you should be holy: You must abstain from sexual immorality; each of you must know how to control his own body in holiness and honor, not in lustful passion like the Gentiles who do not know God; and no one should ever violate or exploit his brother in this regard, because the Lord will avenge all such acts, as we have already told you and solemnly warned you.
verses.where: In the Greek and Roman world a wife was expected to be faithful, while men commonly used slaves and prostitutes without disgrace. Paul writes to new Gentile believers that holiness reaches the body, and he applies the same standard to men and women alike.

verses.text: And that is what some of you were. But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified, in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God.
verses.where: Paul has just listed wrongs that were common in the room, sexual sins beside greed, drunkenness, verbal abuse and theft. Then he speaks to real people: that is what some of you were. The washing has already happened, and it is the ground of the call to live differently.

verses.text: The husband should fulfill his marital duty to his wife, and likewise the wife to her husband. The wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband. Likewise the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife.
verses.where: Answering questions the Corinthians sent him, Paul describes sex in marriage as mutual. Each spouse belongs to the other, and the wife's claim on the husband is stated in the same words as his on her, which was unusual in ancient writing on marriage.

verses.text: Marriage should be honored by all and the marriage bed kept undefiled, for God will judge the sexually immoral and adulterers.
verses.where: In a closing list of ordinary Christian duties, beside hospitality, remembering prisoners and freedom from the love of money, Hebrews asks the whole church to honor marriage and keep it faithful. Sexual faithfulness is treated as everyone's business, not only the married couple's.

verses.text: “No one, Lord,” she answered. “Then neither do I condemn you,” Jesus declared. “Now go and sin no more.”
verses.where: A woman caught in adultery is brought to Jesus to trap him, while the man is nowhere in sight. Jesus sends her accusers away and tells her he does not condemn her, and then tells her to go and sin no more. This story is missing from the earliest manuscripts of John, and many Bibles mark it, but the church has long kept it.

verses.text: Then David said to Nathan, “I have sinned against the LORD.” “The LORD has taken away your sin,” Nathan replied. “You will not die.
verses.where: King David took another man's wife and arranged her husband's death. The prophet Nathan tells him a story about a stolen lamb until David condemns himself. When David confesses, Nathan announces that the LORD has taken away his sin, though the consequences in David's house remain.

misread.taken: “Your body is a temple” has been used to make young people ashamed of their bodies and desires, to treat sexual sin as the one sin that leaves a person permanently damaged, and to shrink the whole of bodily faithfulness down to sex.
misread.says: Paul is answering slogans in Corinth that treated the body as unimportant, as if what it did could not touch the spirit. His answer raises the body's dignity: it belongs to the Lord, it will be raised, and the Spirit lives in it. “You were bought at a price” would have been heard against the slave market, and in a city full of temples it was a striking thing to say about a slave's or a laborer's body. You honor a temple. You do not despise it. The same chapter says that people who had lived far from this were washed (1 Corinthians 6:11).
misread.text: Do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit who is in you, whom you have received from God? You are not your own; you were bought at a price. Therefore glorify God with your body.

misread.taken: This verse is read in two harmful ways: that every passing attraction is already adultery, which leaves people in despair over thoughts they did not choose; or that women must cover and hide so that men will not stumble, which puts the blame on the one who is looked at.
misread.says: The words “to lust after her” describe a look with a purpose, looking in order to want and to take, at least in the mind. Jesus is not speaking about noticing that someone is beautiful, and temptation itself is not sin; Jesus was tempted too. He is naming where sin starts so that it can be stopped there. And he puts the responsibility on the one who looks. He does not tell women to hide; he tells men to guard their own hearts.
misread.text: But I tell you that anyone who looks at a woman to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart.

whole: Few subjects carry as much hidden weight for Christians as this one. Some carry guilt over a past they cannot undo, or a habit they cannot break. Some were raised on warnings so loud that their own bodies came to feel like the enemy, and found that the shame did not lift on their wedding day. Some were abused, and were made to feel, wrongly, that they had lost something. Others look at the church's teaching from the outside, or from the edge, and wonder whether it is anything more than old rules that never fit real lives.

The Bible's account of sex begins with goodness, not danger. A man and a woman are naked and not ashamed; the Song of Songs speaks of desire with more delight than many sermons have dared; Paul describes marriage as two people who belong to each other, and says it in equal terms. The Bible's restrictions grow out of that goodness, not suspicion of it. Sex joins whole persons, Paul argues, so it can never be spiritually neutral. That is why Scripture sets it within the lifelong faithfulness of marriage and calls everything outside that immorality: not because the body is low, but because it is high, bought at a price, and meant to be raised.

That account cuts against more than one set of habits. It cuts against a culture that treats sex as private recreation with no meaning beyond consent, and it cuts against a church culture that taught shame instead of holiness and treated sexual sin as the one stain grace could not reach. Jesus takes the matter further inward than any rulebook, to the look that wants to take, and then sends away the men who came with stones. The same Lord says neither do I condemn you and go and sin no more, and both sentences are meant. Anyone who was abused did not lose purity; the sin was done to them, and it belongs to the one who did it.

So the wisdom here is neither panic nor permission. It begins with honesty about what you keep looking at and what it is doing to you, and with refusing to treat people as things to have. It is carried with others, not alone, because secrecy is where these struggles grow. It sees singleness and marriage as two ways of honoring the body, and gives desire time, as the Song asks. And for every failure it holds out what David heard from Nathan and the Corinthians heard from Paul: confessed sin is taken away, and that is what some of you were. Holiness in the body is not the price of grace. It is what grace begins to do.

differ.share: Christians across the traditions agree that the body is good and will be raised, that sex is God's gift and not something shameful, that it belongs within the faithfulness of marriage, that every person bears God's image and is to be treated with dignity, and that coercion and abuse are always wrong.

views.name: Marriage of a man and a woman
views.body: The historic and still majority reading in the Catholic, Orthodox and most Protestant churches holds that Genesis 1 and 2, Jesus' words in Matthew 19, and Paul's in Romans 1 and 1 Corinthians 6 teach that sexual union belongs only in the marriage of a man and a woman. Every unmarried believer, whatever their attractions, is called to chastity, and the church is called to be family to them.

views.name: Affirming covenanted same-sex marriage
views.body: Some Protestant churches in recent decades hold that the biblical prohibitions addressed practices of the ancient world such as exploitative relations with boys or slaves, not faithful lifelong unions. They hold that the Bible's ethic of covenant faithfulness applies to same-sex couples who marry, and that the call to chastity outside marriage applies to everyone alike.

views.name: Contraception
views.body: Christians also differ on contraception. Catholic teaching holds that each marital act should remain open to the gift of life and rejects artificial contraception, while permitting natural family planning; most Protestant churches and many Orthodox Christians permit contraception within marriage.

differ.after: These are serious questions, and churches divide over them at real cost. A thoughtful Christian on either side should be able to state the other's case in words its holders would sign. All of them call believers to holiness in the body, honesty about desire, and the refusal to treat anyone as less than the image of God.

deep.sit: What would change if you believed your body was not your enemy, and not your own, but the Lord's, bought at a price and meant to be raised?

prayer.lead: A prayer of David that asks God to remember his own love and forget the sins of youth.
prayer.text: Remember, O LORD, Your compassion and loving devotion, for they are from age to age. Remember not the sins of my youth, nor my rebellious acts; remember me according to Your loving devotion, because of Your goodness, O LORD.
